blocks.text: The angle between two vectors \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) is determined from the definition of cross product.
If \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\), then \(|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}| = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\sin\theta\)

blocks.text_alt: sine theta equals the magnitude of a cross b divided by the product of the magnitudes of a and b

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why it works: taking the magnitude of \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = (|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\sin\theta)\underline{n}\) removes \(\underline{n}\) because \(|\underline{n}| = 1\), and \(\sin\theta \ge 0\) for \(0 \le \theta \le \pi\).
Be careful: \(\sin\theta\) alone does not fix \(\theta\), since \(\theta\) and \(180^{\circ} - \theta\) have the same sine. If the angle itself is needed, use \(\cos\theta = \underline{a} \cdot \underline{b}/(|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|)\) from 14.2, or check the sign of \(\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b}\): positive means acute, negative means obtuse.

blocks.title: Example 16
blocks.problem: If \(\underline{a} = 4\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{b} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\). Find a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\). Also find the sine of the angle between the vectors \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{a} = 4\underline{i} + 3\underline{j} + \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{b} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + 2\underline{k}\).
To find: (1) a unit vector perpendicular to both \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\); (2) the sine of the angle between \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\).
Method: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) is perpendicular to both; dividing it by its own length gives a unit vector. Then \(\sin\theta = |\underline{a} \times \underline{b}| / (|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|)\). Both parts need \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) and its magnitude, so we find those first.

Step 1: \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b}\) by the determinant formula
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (6 + 1)\underline{i} - (8 - 2)\underline{j} + (-4 - 6)\underline{k}\]
\[= 7\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}\]
Why: \(\underline{i}\): \(3 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot (-1) = 7\); \(\underline{j}\): \(-(4 \cdot 2 - 1 \cdot 2) = -6\); \(\underline{k}\): \(4 \cdot (-1) - 3 \cdot 2 = -10\).

Step 2: Its magnitude
\[|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}| = \sqrt{7^{2} + (-6)^{2} + (-10)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{49 + 36 + 100} = \sqrt{185}\]
Why: magnitude of \(x\underline{i} + y\underline{j} + z\underline{k}\) is \(\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}}\).

Step 3: The unit vector
A unit vector perpendicular to \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\):
\[\dfrac{\underline{a} \times \underline{b}}{|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|}\]
\[= \dfrac{7\underline{i} - b\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}}{\sqrt{185}}\]
Why: dividing a vector by its own length keeps its direction and makes its length 1. (The book prints \(b\underline{j}\) in the numerator; it must be \(6\underline{j}\): see the correction below.)

Step 4: Magnitudes of \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\)
\[|\underline{a}| = \sqrt{4^{2} + 3^{2} + 1^{2}} = \sqrt{26}\]
\[|\underline{b}| = \sqrt{2^{2} + (-1)^{2} + 2^{2}} = 3\]
Why: the sine formula needs both lengths in the denominator.

Step 5: The sine of the angle
\[\sin\theta = \dfrac{|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|}{|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|}\]
\[= \dfrac{\sqrt{185}}{3\sqrt{26}}\]
Why: solve \(|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}| = |\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\sin\theta\) for \(\sin\theta\). Numerically \(\sin\theta \approx 0.889\), between 0 and 1 as it must be.

Check:
\[\underline{a} \cdot (7\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}) = 28 - 18 - 10 = 0\]
\[\underline{b} \cdot (7\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}) = 14 + 6 - 20 = 0\]
Both are zero, so the vector is perpendicular to both. Also \(\cos\theta = \underline{a} \cdot \underline{b}/(|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|) = 7/(3\sqrt{26})\) and \(\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = (185 + 49)/234 = 1\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 16 the book prints the unit vector as \(\frac{7\underline{i} - b\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}}{\sqrt{185}}\). The middle term must be \(-6\underline{j}\), from \(\underline{a} \times \underline{b} = 7\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}\): the correct unit vector is \(\frac{7\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 10\underline{k}}{\sqrt{185}}\).

blocks.title: Example 17
steps:
Given: unit vectors \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) in the \(xy\)-plane making angles \(\alpha\) and \(-\beta\) with the positive \(x\)-axis.
To prove: \(\sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\).
Method: compute \(\overrightarrow{OB} \times \overrightarrow{OA}\) in two ways: by the definition (gives \(\sin(\alpha + \beta)\)) and by the determinant formula (gives the right-hand side). Equate the two.

Step 1: The angle between them
\[m\angle AOB = \alpha + \beta\]
Why: \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) is \(\alpha\) above the \(x\)-axis and \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) is \(\beta\) below it.

Step 2: Write the vectors in components
\[\overrightarrow{OA} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\]
\[\overrightarrow{OB} = \cos(-\beta)\,\underline{i} + \sin(-\beta)\,\underline{j}\]
\[= \cos\beta\,\underline{i} - \sin\beta\,\underline{j}\]
Why: a unit vector at angle \(\phi\) to the \(x\)-axis is \(\cos\phi\,\underline{i} + \sin\phi\,\underline{j}\); and \(\cos(-\beta) = \cos\beta\), \(\sin(-\beta) = -\sin\beta\).

Step 3: Set up the cross product
\[\overrightarrow{OB} \times \overrightarrow{OA}\]
\[= (\cos\beta\,\underline{i} - \sin\beta\,\underline{j}) \times (\cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{i})\]
Why: substitute the components from Step 2. (The book prints \(\sin\alpha\,\underline{i}\) in the second bracket; it must be \(\sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\), as in Step 2.)

Step 4: Definition on the left, determinant on the right
\[|\overrightarrow{OB}||\overrightarrow{OA}|\sin(\alpha + \beta)\,\underline{k}\]
\[= \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ \cos\beta & -\sin\beta & 0 \\ \cos\alpha & \sin\alpha & 0 \end{vmatrix}\]
Why: both vectors lie in the \(xy\)-plane, so the cross product is along the \(z\)-axis; turning from \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) to \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) is anticlockwise, so by the right hand rule \(\underline{n} = \underline{k}\).

Step 5: Expand the determinant
\[\sin(\alpha + \beta)\,\underline{k}\]
\[= (\sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta)\underline{k}\]
Why: \(|\overrightarrow{OB}| = |\overrightarrow{OA}| = 1\); the \(\underline{i}\)- and \(\underline{j}\)-parts vanish because of the zeros; the \(\underline{k}\)-part is \(\cos\beta\sin\alpha - (-\sin\beta)\cos\alpha\).

Step 6: Compare the coefficients of \(\underline{k}\)
\[\therefore\; \sin(\alpha + \beta) = \sin\alpha\cos\beta + \cos\alpha\sin\beta\]
Why: equal vectors have equal components.

Check:
\(\alpha = \beta = 45^{\circ}\): left side \(\sin 90^{\circ} = 1\); right side \(\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = 1\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Example 17 the second bracket is printed \((\cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{i})\); the second unit vector must be \(\underline{j}\): \(\overrightarrow{OA} = \cos\alpha\,\underline{i} + \sin\alpha\,\underline{j}\). The determinant that follows uses the correct components.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Proof-type examples like 17 and 18 show how vectors prove results of trigonometry. In the exam, write every line with its reason (components, right hand rule, \(|\underline{n}| = 1\)), exactly as in the steps above.

blocks.title: Example 18
blocks.problem: In any triangle \(ABC\), prove that \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}\) (Law of Sines).
steps:
Given: triangle \(ABC\) with vectors \(\underline{a}, \underline{b}, \underline{c}\) along the sides \(BC, CA, AB\).
To prove: \(\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}\) (Law of Sines).
Method: the three vectors go round the triangle, so their sum is \(\underline{0}\). Taking cross products gives equal cross products; equating their magnitudes brings in the sines.

Step 1: Sum of the side vectors
\[\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\]
\[\Rightarrow \underline{b} + \underline{c} = -\underline{a} \quad \text{(i)}\]
Why: going \(B \to C \to A \to B\) returns to the start, so the total displacement is zero.

Step 2: Cross product of (i) with \(\underline{c}\)
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{c} + \underline{c} \times \underline{c} = -\underline{a} \times \underline{c}\]
\[\underline{b} \times \underline{c} = \underline{c} \times \underline{a} \quad (\because\, \underline{c} \times \underline{c} = \underline{0})\]
Why: \(\underline{c} \times \underline{c} = \underline{0}\), and \(-\underline{a} \times \underline{c} = \underline{c} \times \underline{a}\) because reversing the order changes the sign.

Step 3: Equate the magnitudes
\[|\underline{b} \times \underline{c}| = |\underline{c} \times \underline{a}|\]
\[|\underline{b}||\underline{c}|\sin(\pi - A) = |\underline{c}||\underline{a}|\sin(\pi - B)\]
Why: placed tail to tail, \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) make the exterior angle \(\pi - A\), not \(A\) (see the figure); similarly \(\underline{c}\) and \(\underline{a}\) make \(\pi - B\).

Step 4: Simplify
\[bc\sin A = ca\sin B\]
\[\Rightarrow b\sin A = a\sin B\]
\[\therefore\; \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{a}{\sin A} \quad \text{(ii)}\]
Why: \(\sin(\pi - x) = \sin x\), \(|\underline{a}| = a\) etc.; divide by \(c\), then by \(\sin A\sin B\).

Step 5: Similarly, with \(\underline{b}\)
\[\underline{a} \times \underline{b} + \underline{c} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0}\]
\[\Rightarrow \underline{a} \times \underline{b} = \underline{b} \times \underline{c}\]
\[ab\sin(\pi - C) = bc\sin(\pi - A)\]
\[\Rightarrow \dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C} \quad \text{(iii)}\]
Why: cross (\(\underline{a} + \underline{b} + \underline{c} = \underline{0}\)) with \(\underline{b}\), using \(\underline{b} \times \underline{b} = \underline{0}\); the book says only 'Similarly', so these lines are filled in by us.

Step 6: Combine (ii) and (iii)
\[\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}\]
Why: both equations contain \(a/\sin A\).

Check:
In the right triangle with sides \(3, 4, 5\): \(5/\sin 90^{\circ} = 5\), \(3/(3/5) = 5\), \(4/(4/5) = 5\).

blocks.title: Example 19
blocks.problem: If \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\) and \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\), find by determinant formula (i) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u}\) (ii) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\) (iii) \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\).
steps:
Given: \(\underline{u} = 2\underline{i} - \underline{j} + \underline{k}\), \(\underline{v} = 4\underline{i} + 2\underline{j} - \underline{k}\).
To find: (i) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u}\), (ii) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\), (iii) \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) by the determinant formula.
Method: row 2 = first vector, row 3 = second vector in each part; the answers can be checked against the properties.

(i) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u}\)
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix} = \underline{0}\]
Why: two identical rows make the determinant zero (the book: 'Two rows are same'); this is the property \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \underline{0}\).

(ii) \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v}\)
\[\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (1 - 2)\underline{i} - (-2 - 4)\underline{j} + (4 + 4)\underline{k}\]
\[= -\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k}\]
Why: \(\underline{i}\): \((-1)(-1) - (1)(2)\); \(\underline{j}\): \(-[(2)(-1) - (1)(4)]\); \(\underline{k}\): \((2)(2) - (-1)(4)\). (Same vectors as Example 15.)

(iii) \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\)
\[\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = \begin{vmatrix} \underline{i} & \underline{j} & \underline{k} \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}\]
\[= (2 - 1)\underline{i} - (4 + 2)\underline{j} + (-4 - 4)\underline{k}\]
\[= \underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 8\underline{k}\]
Why: now \(\underline{v}\) comes first, so it goes in row 2.

Check:
\[\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\]
\(\underline{i} - 6\underline{j} - 8\underline{k} = -(-\underline{i} + 6\underline{j} + 8\underline{k})\), as the property \(\underline{u} \times \underline{v} = -\underline{v} \times \underline{u}\) says.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\sin\theta = \frac{|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|}{|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|}\); compare \(\cos\theta = \frac{\underline{a} \cdot \underline{b}}{|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|}\).
2. A unit vector perpendicular to \(\underline{a}\) and \(\underline{b}\) is \(\pm\frac{\underline{a} \times \underline{b}}{|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|}\).
3. Vectors along the sides of a triangle add to \(\underline{0}\); the angle between two such vectors is an exterior angle \(\pi - A\).
4. \(\underline{v} \times \underline{u} = -(\underline{u} \times \underline{v})\) and \(\underline{u} \times \underline{u} = \underline{0}\), as Example 19 shows.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Dividing by \(|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|\) instead of \(|\underline{a}||\underline{b}|\) in the sine formula.
2. Taking \(\theta\) from the sine alone when the angle may be obtuse.
3. In Example 18, using the interior angle \(A\) instead of \(\pi - A\) between \(\underline{b}\) and \(\underline{c}\) (the result is the same only because \(\sin(\pi - A) = \sin A\)).
4. Forgetting that only one of the two unit normals is asked; \(-\frac{\underline{a} \times \underline{b}}{|\underline{a} \times \underline{b}|}\) is equally correct.
